title: Choosing a practice
hook: fit, a good teacher, community, and an ethical frame

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was closed practices, rites a community keeps for its own. Your line was not mine to take.

A shoe store, a Saturday afternoon. The runner on the bench has tried on six pairs. One pair is beautiful and pinches. One is what a famous athlete wears and slides off the heel. Finally the salesperson says something useful: walk to the back of the store and back, and tell me which one you forget you're wearing. After weeks visiting the world's schools of practice, a fair question is waiting. Which of these, if any, would you actually wear every day? Not the most impressive. Not the one a friend swears by. The one that fits.
screen: `SIX PAIRS ON THE BENCH.` → `THE ONE YOU FORGET YOU'RE WEARING.` → `WHICH WOULD YOU WEAR DAILY?`

segments.voice: Four questions, each worth slowing down for. First, fit. Does this practice suit your body, your temperament, your days? Someone with a bad knee may not sit cross-legged for an hour. Someone who thinks best while moving might find walking or slow movement easier than stillness. Someone who loves words may be drawn to reading and reflection. Fit isn't laziness: a practice you can keep beats a grand one you abandon. Second, a good teacher. Not a famous one: someone who has done the practice a long time, is honest about its limits, and welcomes your questions. Third, community. Practice is easier in company, and company keeps you honest. A group that sits, sings or studies together will notice when you stop showing up. Fourth, an ethical frame. Several schools on this tour came with one: precepts, commandments, virtues, vows. A technique without a way of living around it can drift. Two old texts give a way to test all four. In the Buddhist Kalama Sutta, in paraphrase, the Buddha tells a group of confused villagers not to go by rumor, tradition or a teacher's reputation alone, but to notice for themselves which things lead to harm and which to well-being, and choose accordingly. And in the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus gives a short test for telling true prophets from false: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." Each text speaks in its own setting, and each asks you to watch what a practice actually grows in a person, over time.
screen: `FIT: BODY, TEMPERAMENT, DAYS.` · `A TEACHER WHO WELCOMES QUESTIONS.` · `COMPANY KEEPS YOU HONEST.` · `AN ETHICAL FRAME AROUND IT.` · then, large: `KNOW THEM BY THEIR FRUITS.`

segments.voice: Take the four questions one by one, slowly. What fits your body and your days right now, not in some ideal year? What would you want from a teacher, do you need company or quiet, and what way of living would you want a practice to sit inside? Let one honest word come for each; it doesn't have to be a good answer.
Choosing a practice. Four questions: fit, a good teacher, community, and an ethical frame, tested by what the practice grows in a person. Today's word.
Your line: what fits. A practice you can keep beats a grand one you abandon. See you on the path.

howItsDone: People choosing a practice often try several, look for a teacher with long experience who welcomes questions, join a group that practices together, and keep the practice inside an ethical frame such as precepts, commandments or vows; in some traditions a newcomer simply starts by attending and asking.

chat.says: How do I know which spiritual practice is right for me?
options: Ask about fit, a good teacher, community and ethics, then watch what it grows in you.
Pick the one with the most famous teacher, since fame shows a practice really works.
Go with whatever feels most intense, since the hardest practice is always the best.
chat.meaning: Four questions: fit, a good teacher, community and an ethical frame. The Kalama Sutta and Matthew both ask you to watch what a practice grows.

Kalama Sutta.meaning: a Buddhist teaching to villagers on testing what they hear

Buddha.meaning: the awakened one, whose teachings Buddhists follow

precepts.meaning: basic rules for how to live

Matthew.meaning: one of the four Gospels about the life of Jesus

sources.quoted: Ye shall know them by their fruits.

notes: The Kalama Sutta is paraphrased. Confirm the numbering (AN 3.65) and that the paraphrase (not going by rumor, tradition or a teacher's reputation alone; noticing what leads to harm and to well-being) is fair, and not stretched into a general license to ignore tradition.
Matthew 7:16 is quoted from the KJV; in context Jesus is speaking of false prophets. The script calls it 'a short test for teachers', which a Christian reviewer should confirm is fair.
The script says 'Several schools on this tour came with' an ethical frame, referring to the path's own Block F days.
The four questions come from the index line. No claim is made about which practice suits whom; the examples (bad knee, thinking while moving, loving words) are illustrative only.
Editor pass: Matthew 7:16 now framed as a test for telling true prophets from false, as in its context, not 'a test for teachers'.
